title: The righteous shall live by faith (Romans 1:17)
hookLine: a tormented monk named Luther reads Romans and feels the gates of paradise open

cards: A friar kneels in confession, and he's been there a long time. He lists his sins, remembers more, and goes back.
He fasts, prays through the night, follows the rule of his order to the letter, and still can't shake the feeling that God is a judge waiting to condemn him.
His name is Martin Luther, a monk who teaches the Bible at the university in Wittenberg. Looking back years later, he wrote that one phrase in Paul's letter to the Romans had become hateful to him.

teach.h: THE JUST SHALL LIVE BY FAITH.
teach.b: Here's the verse, in the King James Bible, Romans chapter one: "For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith."
As it is written: Paul is quoting the prophet Habakkuk, who says, "the just shall live by his faith." The phrase Luther hated was the righteousness of God.
He'd been taught to hear it, he says, as God's own justice, the righteousness by which God punishes the unrighteous. And if that's what the gospel reveals, how is it good news?

So he kept beating at the verse, his word, until he saw it differently. The righteousness of God here, he came to think, isn't what God demands of people but what God gives them: a gift, received by trusting it.

In his own telling, he felt born again, as if he'd walked through open gates into paradise itself, and the whole Bible looked different afterward. Christians still disagree about how faith and good works fit together.
Lutherans and other Protestants stress that people are made right with God by grace through faith, as a gift.
Catholic and Orthodox teaching also says it is all grace, and speaks of faith working through love, growing over a lifetime.
Today, Catholic and Lutheran churches have signed a joint statement saying they share a basic understanding here, while still differing in emphasis.
But the moment in the study belongs to Luther: a frightened man, a single verse, and gates he hadn't known were open.

how: Justification by faith is a central theme of Lutheran teaching, and Christians across traditions study Romans together, often reading Paul alongside the prophet he quotes.

games.q: you're Luther. one phrase in Romans terrifies you every time you read it. what do you do?
o: skip that chapter and teach something else.
keep beating at the verse until it opens.
ask the head of your monastery and accept his answer.
games.why: he kept beating at it, he says, until he saw the righteousness of God as a gift, and felt he'd walked through open gates into paradise.

practice: Say the verse in your head, the just shall live by faith; then again, leaning on just; again, leaning on live; and then only the last two words, by faith.
Notice which word you lean on, and whether it sounds like a demand or a gift today; there's no right answer. If you pray, let the line become a prayer as it is; if you don't, just let it sit.

wordCard.voice: Habakkuk. The prophet Paul quotes in Romans: the just shall live by faith, the verse Luther first heard as a threat and then as a gift.

orig.note: Greek: faith, trust. Romans 1:17 says the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith.

carryVoice: Your line: the gates opened. Some things can only be received, never earned. Day eight hundred fifty-two, done.
